en: [Introduction] I shall explain the duties for those beings, such as deceased masters, who are practitioners of Vajrasattva and the like, by way of showing them the path during their intermediate state. (1)
[Inauspicious outcomes in the case that the funeral rite is not performed:

If the emission of the Knowledge Being (*jñānasattva*) and so forth is not performed for them, there would be the consequence of the destruction of their stūpas; therefore, their bodies must be cremated. (2)
There are nine gates for the emergence of consciousness:
the head, the bindu, as well as the ears, the eyes, the nose, and the mouth. (3)

The navel, the anus, and the opening of the lower wind—when consciousness departs from these, the wise know it as the state of misfortune; but when consciousness departs through the crown of the head, the wise know it as the auspicious state.
If one should go by means of the *bindu*, one is born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); if there is a transition through the navel, one's destination will be the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Through the two ears one attains birth in the Siddha-yoni; through the nose, one becomes a Yakṣa;
through the eyes, one attains the status of a king among men.
If he should depart through the mouth, he will certainly go to the womb of a preta;
or if he should go by way of the urinary passage, it is proclaimed that he will take birth as an animal.
If the consciousness of living beings should travel by the path of ruin, it will take birth in the eight terrible hells; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (8)
Indeed, having correctly understood women as being merely reflections of the male body,
and having discerned the point of exit for consciousness, the wise man [proceeds].
[The Funeral Procession] The preceptor, having recited the true vidyā and being devoted to the three samādhis,
follows accompanied by the tumultuous sound of the loud drum, song, and instrumental music. (10)

Having brought the corpse to the cremation ground by a path strewn with heaps of flowers, parched grain, and gold, preceded by the offering of a sacrificial oblation (bali), [he performed the rites]. 11.
On a level, pure plot of ground smeared with cow dung,
one should have a square mandala made; there, one should scatter [the colored powders].
There, having raised up with a wooden stylus either white or yellow powder— which resembles the petals of a lotus— one should draw a brilliantly shining vajra in the center.
One should draw a wheel on the eastern petal, and a jewel on the southern;
a lotus flower on the western, and likewise a sword on the northern.
Having drawn a goad in the southeast, a noose in the southwest, a thunderbolt in the northwest corners, and a blue lotus in the northeast, one should draw them. 15.
Or else, it should be white in color, adorned with archways and the like, square in shape, having four doors, and beautified by eight pillars. || 16 ||
Having drawn a mandala joined with petals from the corners,
there are nineteen deities in the Viśvābja-maṇḍala for the rite of pacification.
Alternatively, one should draw there the thirty-two emblems of the deities;
or should one draw them upon the food?
[Abhiṣeka]
Facing north, the mantra-practitioner, having fully worshipped the mandala, [should offer] the bali.
Having offered the *argha* and other honors and having successfully completed the mandala,
the adept should station [the deity] at the eastern gate of the mandala, facing south.
Having placed the corpse within one's own heart and [visualized] the seed-syllable with its multitude of light-rays,
[one should contemplate] that evil karma which produces the terrible cycle of existence.
One should destroy [the obstacles] with masses of wrathful deities and flashing vajra-weapons;
then, having summoned the consciousness through the application of mantra and mudrā, [one should proceed]. (21)
Then, having caused [the disciple] to enter by means of the goad and other implements, one should again bestow the consecrations and so forth;
[this applies whether the soul] is bound by the latent impressions of its own karma and situated wherever it may be.
Having summoned the Jñānasattva, one should cause him to enter the dead body:
"Jaḥ! O Vajrāṅkuśa! Hūṃ! O Vajrapāśa! Vaṃ! O Vajrasphoṭa! Hoḥ! O Vajraghaṇṭā! || 23 ||
Then the master himself, entering with the mindset of a disciple—
[or rather,] with the mindset of a disciple regarding the food—
having received here the permission from his own lord, he should perform the consecration and so forth.
In the same way, one should offer everything, including the *jaya* and other vases, even for a corpse;
having bestowed the consecration up to the final authorization, one should behold the *jñānasattva*.

Having given food, one should bestow the empowerment; then, having [visualized] the form of Vajrasattva and so forth, who possesses the vajras of body, speech, and mind, as well as Kṣitigarbha and others, and Locanā and others, one should then present the water for honoring (argha) and the other offerings. || 26 ||
Having understood that song, instrumental music, flowers, incense, and even the food offering are in every way of a pleasing nature, one should then dismiss [the deity].
[The Utkrānti]:

By means of the Locanā and other goddesses, drawn forth by the array of light from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, together with hosts of fully enlightened Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and heroic Vīriṇīs; || 28 ||
Beholding the surface of the sky filled with Siddhas, Gandharvas, serpents, gods, and even Vidyādharas, as a rain of flowers fell from above, [he was amazed]. (29)
It was adorned with the sound of divine drums, the resonance of mṛdaṅgas and mardalas,
and embellished by the sweet tones of flutes, lutes, and other instruments raised aloft.
Then, by performing a brilliant dance through the great expansion of bliss,
they draw forth consciousness and lead it to the realm called Sukhāvatī and others.
Having established [the image] within the world-system as a support for the Buddhas and their sons,
the wise one, having beheld it from that point for the sake of its long-term preservation,
should joyfully recite this mantra, having made the Tathāgatas witnesses. (32)

Oṃ supratiṣṭhitavajre svāhā. Immediately thereafter, one should bathe [the image] with the waters from the Vijayā and other jars. Having observed the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) upon the funeral pyre in the same manner as the pacification pit (śāntikuṇḍa), one should perform the fire offering (homa). || 33 ||
[The Cremation:

Having observed the fire and other elements as before, and having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should then visualize Vajrasattva and the others within the fire and present the water for honor (argha) and so forth. (34)
Then, one who is proud of wisdom should offer oblation upon the vajra-tongue to that Jñānasattva in the heart, which is blazing with white rays of light. (35)
Having offered an oblation filled with ghee, one should then offer oblations of rice and other grains;
having again offered a full oblation, one should speak these words: || 36 ||
Oṃ vajrānala, make the body of [Name] Vajra immortal, svāhā.
Having offered water for sipping and sprinkling, and having worshipped with flowers and other offerings,
[one should perform the rite] together with his mantra, mudrās, armor, and vajra.
Having brought forth the empowerment of Kṣitigarbha and the others, which consists of the vajras of body, speech, and mind, the mandala master should cause them to enter into his own self. (38)
Having fashioned a true wheel from wood in the shape of Kubera’s head,
and having placed it upon the funeral pyre, one should then cover it again with wood.
One should scatter heaps of flowers according to the method for imparting the taste of nectar;
having properly rendered the corpse into nectar, one should offer it to the Svādhipati.
Oṃ amṛtāsvādavajra svāhā.
Then, having mentally gratified [the deities], the wise one performs the rinsing of the mouth for the deity. || 41 ||
Oṃ hrīḥ suviśuddhadharma ācamanaṃ kuru svāhā.
Having cast flowers and other offerings there, one should dismiss them with this verse: || 42 ||
Oṃ! You have accomplished the welfare of all sentient beings; success has been granted according to your aspirations.
Go now to the realm of the Buddhas, and return once more. 43.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ vajra muḥ. Having thus consecrated the corpse and having dismissed the fire deity,
Then, one should give a small stool to those beings who have turned away and so forth. || 44 ||
One should likewise perform the *gaṇacakra* according to the ritual rules for seven days;
and on the third day, those auspicious white *siddhārtha* seeds [should be offered]. (45)
Anointed with fragrant sandalwood and empowered by one hundred and eight recitations of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā mantra, one should strike this bone. 46.
O noble one, by reciting this *Asitā-dhāraṇī*, or even by muttering the *Pratisarā*,
or also by [reciting] the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī*...
Alternatively, having recited the Vimaloṣṇīṣa [sūtra], one should strike with grains of sand. || 47 ||
One should strike it with bone fragments or with a sesame seed-cake;
by this means, even if it has been discarded anywhere, it will become [effective]. (48)
Whether at the ocean or a river, one who has died is reborn in a happy state after the heap of bones has been gathered and bathed with milk, perfumes, and other substances. (49)
Having performed a vigil for him with flowers, incense, music, and other offerings,
one should construct a shrine containing his bones, adorned with a series of parasols.
The funerary *caitya* is mounted upon a staff and adorned with *chudhākṣauda*;
however, this sequence is taught according to the tradition of the manifest Ācāryas. (51)
But when the assembly of beings is well-guarded, one should create such [an emanation] through meditation alone.
Having performed this rite, one should offer the sacrificial fee consisting of a communal meal and so forth. (52)

Having given [the food] and transformed it, one should dedicate that merit toward the enlightenment of all. By such a procedure regarding the food, a person who dies while in its presence [attains the goal]. 53.

This conceptualization called "death" is led to the state of the Sky-farer (khecarī), because of the profundity of dependent origination and the infinity of the cognitions of phenomena; therefore, all that is to be done has been accomplished by the wise, and it is to be trusted. 54.
The section on the karma of internal duration.
